opus-5.5.text:
Well, the key thing is what happens after the prediction. When I talk about prediction in the sense that matters for intelligence, I mean you predict something about the world, then the world actually unfolds, and you find out whether you were right. If you were wrong, you're surprised, and you learn from that surprise. You adjust. That's the essence of it: a prediction is something that can be checked against what really happens, and that checking drives learning.

Now, with a large language model, you can ask it, "What do you think the user will say next?" and it will produce some text. But that's not a prediction in this substantive sense. It's not going to be surprised when the user says something different. It doesn't change its understanding of the world based on the mismatch. There's no ground truth it's held accountable to during its ongoing life. It's just generating the kind of thing a person might say in that situation, because it was trained to mimic what people say.

So what it has is a model of what people would say, not a model of the world. Those are very different things. A model of the world lets you predict the consequences of your actions and then learn when the consequences turn out differently. The language model doesn't have a goal, it doesn't have consequences in that sense, and it doesn't learn from its experience while it's interacting. It learned from a fixed corpus of human text, and then it's frozen.

To me, real prediction is part of a loop: you act, you predict, you observe, you're right or wrong, and you update. Without that loop, calling the output a "prediction" is really just a manner of speaking. It's imitation dressed up in the language of anticipation.

r001.rationale: The response says the language model will not be surprised when the user says something different and does not update its understanding from the mismatch, identifying this failure to adjust as why its output is not substantive prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me put it this way. When you ask a language model to anticipate what a user will say next, what you're really getting is a mimic of what a person would say in that situation. It's imitating the actions of a person. But prediction in the sense I care about is about the world. It's about what will happen as a consequence of what you do. The model has no ground truth there. It makes its guess, and then nothing happens to it. There's no surprise. Nothing comes back and says, "You were wrong about that." The actual user response arrives, and the model doesn't learn from it. It's not updating anything. It's not changing its weights in response to the outcome.

A real prediction has a definite thing it's about, and there's a moment when you find out whether you were right. That's what makes it substantive. That's what gives you the possibility of learning from experience. A squirrel predicts where the nut is, goes there, and either finds it or doesn't. That's prediction, and it has consequences for the squirrel.

So what the language model is doing is next-token prediction on a corpus of human text. That's a prediction task, yes, in the engineering sense, but it's a prediction about what humans wrote, not about the world. And there's no goal in it. There's no notion of what the right thing to say is, except that it's what a person would say. Without a goal, you can't really have a sense of right and wrong. And without a sense of right and wrong, you don't have the basis for an intelligence that's learning. You have a very sophisticated form of imitation. I think that's an important distinction, and it's one the field is in danger of glossing over.

r001.rationale: The response says the model receives no feedback when its guess is wrong and does not learn or update its weights in response to the actual outcome, identifying this failure to adjust as why its prediction is not substantive.

astra-6.text:
Well, it is prediction in a literal sense. I wouldn’t want to deny that. The question is whether the prediction is being tested against what actually happens. You can ask a language model, “What will the user say next?” and it will produce something plausible. But producing a plausible answer isn’t the same as demonstrating that you can reliably anticipate the user’s response.

What I’m interested in is a system that makes predictions, observes the consequences, and learns from the discrepancy. If it anticipates that the user will respond in one way and the user responds differently, does that experience change its future predictions? Is there an ongoing process that makes its expectations more accurate?

So the issue isn’t whether the output can be called a prediction. It’s whether prediction is functioning as a connection between the system and its experience, with the world supplying the correction.

r001.rationale: The response says substantive prediction should involve learning from discrepancies, but it does not state that a large language model fails to adjust when events contradict its apparent predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I wouldn’t say it isn’t prediction at all. Predicting what someone will say is a perfectly legitimate prediction problem. The question is what that demonstrates. If you ask a language model, “What will the user say next?” it produces some text. That by itself doesn’t tell you whether it has made an accurate prediction. You have to wait for the user’s response and compare the two.

And then there’s the question of learning from that comparison. Does the system register that its expectation was wrong and change its future expectations? In the systems I’m interested in, predictions are grounded in an ongoing stream of experience. You make a prediction, experience supplies an outcome, and the discrepancy drives learning.

So I’d distinguish generating a plausible answer to a prediction question from demonstrating a reliable, continually improving ability to anticipate what actually happens. The first can be part of the second, but it doesn’t establish it.

r001.rationale: The response says substantive prediction requires the system to register when its expectation is wrong and update future expectations from the discrepancy; merely generating a plausible prediction does not establish that ability.
